title: Amplitude equations for wave bifurcations in reaction-diffusion systems
abstract: A wave bifurcation is the counterpart to a Turing instability in reaction-diffusion systems, but where the critical wavenumber corresponds to a pure imaginary pair rather than a zero temporal eigenvalue. Such bifurcations require at least three components and give rise to patterns that are periodic in both space and time. Depending on boundary conditions, these patterns can comprise either rotating or standing waves. Restricting to systems in one spatial dimension, complete formulae are derived for the evaluation of the coefficients of the weakly nonlinear normal form of the bifurcation up to order five, including those that determine the criticality of both rotating and standing waves. The formulae apply to arbitrary $n$-component systems ($n\geq 3$) and their evaluation is implemented in software which is made available as supplementary material. The theory is illustrated on two different versions of three-component reaction-diffusion models of excitable media that were previously shown to feature super- and subcritical wave instabilities and on a five-component model of two-layer chemical reaction. In each case, two-parameter bifurcation diagrams are produced to illustrate the connection between complex dispersion relations and different types of Hopf, Turing, and wave bifurcations, including the existence of several codimension-two bifurcations.
summary: This theoretical paper develops comprehensive mathematical tools to analyze wave bifurcations in complex reaction-diffusion systems. It derives the weakly nonlinear normal form equations up to the fifth order, providing explicit formulas for the coefficients that determine whether the resulting waves are supercritical or subcritical. This work significantly advances the mathematical understanding of pattern formation in non-equilibrium physical models.
main_problem: The paper aims to derive general amplitude equations for wave bifurcations in reaction-diffusion systems, which are counterparts to Turing instabilities.
main_result: Complete formulae for the weakly nonlinear normal form coefficients up to order five are derived for both standing and rotating wave solutions in arbitrary n-component systems.
method: The analysis employs a multi-scale asymptotic methodology, extending normal-form analysis from Hopf and Turing bifurcations to derive amplitude equations for the system's modes.
model_or_system: The study concerns general n-component reaction-diffusion systems ($\partial_t u = f(u, \mu) + D(\mu) \partial_{xx} u$) exhibiting wave bifurcations, which require at least three components.
key_observables: The coefficients of the weakly nonlinear normal form (e.g., $C[\cdot]$) and the resulting bifurcation diagrams characterizing the stability and type (super/subcritical) of standing and travelling waves.
important_parameters: The number of components ($n \geq 3$), the bifurcation parameter ($\mu$), and the spatial/temporal wave number ($k^*$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the existence of a stable, isolated homogeneous steady state and relies on non-degeneracy conditions to perform the asymptotic expansions.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the difference between dispersion relations for Turing (real eigenvalue) and wave (pure imaginary pair) bifurcations. Figure 2 summarizes the parameter space region showing the bifurcation type (SW/TW) based on cubic coefficients.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the general framework for wave bifurcations, then deriving the normal form equations up to fifth order, and finally analyzing the coefficients to determine the precise nature (supercritical vs. subcritical) of the resulting wave patterns.
why_interesting: While focused on classical reaction-diffusion systems, the rigorous mathematical machinery of deriving high-order normal forms and analyzing pattern formation stability is highly relevant to understanding the dynamics of open quantum systems or complex many-body dynamics where pattern formation or phase transitions occur.
